name: Taiping Rebellion
info: The Taiping Rebellion was a civil war of 1850–1864 in which the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom of Hong Xiuquan, seeking to overthrow the Qing dynasty and remake Chinese society and religion, ruled much of southern China from Nanjing before its defeat.

facts.where: Southern and central China: Guangxi, where it began at Jintian; Hunan, Hubei, Jiangxi and Anhui along the Yangtze; Nanjing, its capital as Tianjing; southern Jiangsu and Zhejiang, the wealthiest region of the empire; with remnants in Fujian, Guangdong, Sichuan and on the Sino-Vietnamese border.
facts.period: The God Worshipping Society from 1844; the Jintian uprising, 1850–1851; the march north and down the Yangtze, 1851–1853; the Heavenly Kingdom at Nanjing, 1853–1864, with the failed Northern Expedition and the Tianjing Incident of 1856; the siege and fall of Nanjing, 1862–1864; the last Taiping forces, defeated in 1866 and 1871.
facts.figures: Hong Xiuquan, the Heavenly King; Feng Yunshan, founder of the God Worshipping Society; Yang Xiuqing, who claimed to speak as God the Father; Xiao Chaogui; Wei Changhui; Shi Dakai; Hong Rengan, Hong’s cousin; Li Xiucheng, the Loyal King; against them Zeng Guofan of the Xiang Army, Zuo Zongtang and Li Hongzhang.
facts.outcome: The Heavenly Kingdom destroyed with the fall of Nanjing in July 1864, in a war whose dead are most widely estimated at 20 to 30 million; a Qing dynasty weakened in central China and forced to rely on Han gentry and their provincial armies; the Self-Strengthening Movement.

t: Hong Xiuquan, a Hakka who had failed the imperial examinations, came to believe from visions and Christian pamphlets that he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ, sent to rid the world of demons, among them the Qing.

From Nanjing, renamed Tianjing, the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom ruled nearly 30 million people at its peak and announced radical reforms: strict separation of the sexes, the abolition of foot binding, land socialisation and a ban on opium.
Fought as a total war with extreme brutality on both sides, it was the deadliest civil war in history: the most widely cited estimates give 20 to 30 million dead, others as many as 100 million.
dyk: Hong Xiuquan had studied the Bible in Guangzhou with the American Baptist missionary Issachar Jacox Roberts, who refused to baptise him; in 1861 Roberts came to Nanjing, and Hong made him his director of foreign affairs.
ev: Hong Huoxiu fails the imperial examination for the third time and has the visions in which he is given the name Hong Xiuquan
Hong’s follower Feng Yunshan founds the God Worshipping Society in Guangxi
After routing Qing forces at Jintian, Hong declares himself Heavenly King of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom
The Taipings capture Nanjing, rename it Tianjing and kill its Manchu population
In the Tianjing Incident Yang Xiuqing and his followers are slaughtered on Hong Xiuquan’s orders
Zeng Guofan’s Xiang Army captures Anqing, helped by a Royal Navy blockade
Hong Xiuquan dies during the siege, and Nanjing falls to the imperial armies in the Third Battle of Nanjing
The last Taiping army, led by Li Fuzhong, is wiped out on the borders of Hunan, Guizhou and Guangxi

sections.background:
In the 19th century the Qing dynasty suffered famines, natural disasters, economic trouble and defeats by foreign powers. China’s population had nearly doubled between 1766 and 1833 while the cultivated land stayed the same; farmers were heavily overtaxed, rents rose and peasants deserted their land in droves. Defeat in the First Opium War and the illicit importation of opium harmed the economy, banditry became common, and secret societies and self-defence units multiplied. The government, commanded by Manchus, had grown corrupt and was weak in the south, where anti-Manchu feeling was strongest among the Hakka, a Han Chinese subgroup, and where Christian missionaries were active.

In 1837 Hong Huoxiu, a Hakka from a poor village in Guangdong, failed the imperial examination for the third time and suffered a breakdown, in which he dreamed of visiting Heaven and meeting a celestial family; his heavenly father gave him the name Hong Xiuquan. After a fourth and final failure in 1843 he read Christian pamphlets he had received from a Protestant missionary and concluded that his father in the dream was God the Father, his elder brother Jesus Christ, and that he was to rid the world of demons, among them the corrupt Qing government and Confucian teachings. In 1847 he studied the Bible in Guangzhou with the American Baptist missionary Issachar Jacox Roberts, who refused to baptise him.
sections.aims:
Hong sought the religious conversion of the Han people to his syncretic Christianity, the political overthrow of the Qing dynasty and a general transformation of the state; rather than replace China’s ruling class, the Taiping sought to upend the social order. The God Worshipping Society joined Christianity with Taoism, Confucianism and indigenous millenarianism, which Hong presented as a restoration of the ancient Chinese faith in Shangdi. It held that Hong was the second son of God and the younger brother of Jesus, and it called the Manchus demons, against whom a holy war would establish paradise on earth.

The Heavenly Kingdom announced social reforms: strict separation of the sexes, even of married couples, the abolition of foot binding, land socialisation and the suppression of private trade, and it outlawed the importation of opium. Its faith replaced Confucianism, Buddhism and Chinese folk religion; idols were destroyed, Buddhist and Confucian libraries burned, temples defaced or turned to the new religion, and sellers of Confucian works executed. The rebels refused to shave their foreheads and wear the queue, and so were called the Long-Hairs. In modern China the war is often called the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom Movement, and the scholar Jian Youwen speaks of a “Taiping Revolutionary Movement”, because it worked toward a complete change of the political and social system.
sections.events:
The rising began in Guangxi when local officials persecuted the God Worshipping Society. In early January 1851 a rebel army of 10,000 organised by Feng Yunshan and Wei Changhui routed Qing forces at Jintian, and on January 11 Hong declared the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom. Marching north into Hunan and down the Yangtze, the Taipings took Wuchang in December 1852 and Anqing in February 1853, and on March 19, 1853 they captured Nanjing. The Northern Expedition against Beijing failed completely; the Western Expedition had limited success.

Hong withdrew to rule by proclamation, and his suspicion of Yang Xiuqing ended in the Tianjing Incident of 1856, when Yang and his followers were slaughtered on Hong’s orders. Zeng Guofan’s Xiang Army retook Wuchang in December 1856 and Jiujiang in 1858. In 1860 the Taipings broke the imperial siege of Nanjing and took Changzhou and Suzhou, but their attacks on Shanghai were repulsed with the help of the Ever Victorious Army. Zeng took Anqing in 1861 and besieged Nanjing from May 1862. Hong died in June 1864, and Nanjing fell in July after street-by-street fighting. Resistance went on in the highlands of the south until 1866, and the last Taiping army was wiped out in August 1871.
sections.people:
Hong Xiuquan, the Heavenly King, was a Hakka villager who had failed the imperial examinations four times; from 1853 he lived in luxury with many women in his inner chamber and ruled by written proclamations. Feng Yunshan founded the God Worshipping Society, and two other God Worshippers claimed to speak for the Celestial Family, Yang Xiuqing as God the Father and Xiao Chaogui as Jesus Christ. Wei Changhui and Qin Rigang killed Yang in 1856 and were executed by Hong. Shi Dakai, whose family Wei and Qin had killed, led his army west and was executed by slow slicing near Chengdu in 1863. Hong’s cousin Hong Rengan came to Nanjing in 1859 with plans to expand the kingdom, and Li Xiucheng, the Loyal King, advised the Qing before his execution to buy and copy the best foreign cannon.

The rebels came almost entirely from the lowest classes: Hakka, people of Guangdong and Zhuang at first, many of them former miners, and later the people of the Yangtze delta. Women served in large numbers in the early years, led by commanders such as Hong Xuanjiao, Su Sanniang and Qiu Ersao. Against them stood Zeng Guofan, who recruited, paid and drilled village soldiers for the Xiang Army, Zuo Zongtang and Li Hongzhang, and the Ever Victorious Army of Frederick Townsend Ward and Charles George Gordon.
sections.outcomes:
The Taiping were defeated by decentralised provincial armies such as the Xiang Army. The kingdom had been weakened by its internal conflicts after the failed campaign against Beijing and the killings of 1856, and its later leaders failed both to widen their support and to win alliances with the European powers, which stayed officially neutral while European advisers served with the Qing. The landowning class, alarmed by the Taiping ideology and the separation of the sexes, sided with the government, and traditionalist rural classes resisted its hostility to Confucian values. Jonathan Spence counts its failure to coordinate with other rebellions as a key reason for its defeat.

The cost was immense. It was a total war, fought with extreme brutality on both sides, each destroying the other’s farmland and butchering the people of captured cities. The Taiping killed the Manchu population of every area they took, about 40,000 Manchu civilians at Nanjing alone; the Qing massacred civilians, above all at Nanjing, and after the kingdom’s collapse one million are reported to have been executed in Guangdong in massacres of Hakkas. With no reliable census, the most widely cited estimates give 20 to 30 million dead, most of them from plague and famine, and others as many as 73 to 100 million; thirty million people fled.
sections.legacy:
The rebellion is widely considered the most important event in 19th-century Chinese history. By destroying most of the Manchu quarters of southern China, it forced the Qing court to rely on Han gentry and their Yong Ying militias; power was decentralised to a limited extent, and Han officials held high posts more widely than before. By 1865 five of the eight viceroys were Hunanese. The war prompted the Self-Strengthening Movement, and Franz H. Michael saw the gentry militias as the forerunners of the private armies of the warlords who dominated China after the Qing, a claim that Diana Lary cited studies doubting.

Famine, disease and massacres depopulated the Yangtze delta, which was resettled by migrants from Henan; labour became more valuable than land, and refugees helped the economic rise of Shanghai. The Taiping mix of Christianity and radical social equality influenced Sun Yat-sen, and Chinese Communist historians, following Mao Zedong, called the rising proto-communist; John King Fairbank compared the Taiping with Mao’s communists. Its name is still debated: Tobie Meyer-Fong and Stephen Platt argued in 2013 that “rebellion” favours the Qing and that the war should be called a civil war, and Jürgen Osterhammel calls it the Taiping Revolution. Only about a tenth of the Taiping records survive.

summary: The Taiping Rebellion (1850–1864) was a civil war between the Qing dynasty and the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom of Hong Xiuquan, who believed himself the younger brother of Jesus Christ and set out to overthrow the Qing and remake Chinese society. Ruling much of southern China from Nanjing, the kingdom was defeated by provincial armies such as Zeng Guofan’s Xiang Army, in a war that killed an estimated 20 to 30 million people or more.
notes: References: the saved article’s Sources, Modern monographs, Primary sources and Further reading sections are all empty, so references is []. Works named in the text (Fairbank, Spence, Meyer-Fong and Platt, Osterhammel, Michael, Lary) are cited by name only, without titles.

Start 1850: the article dates the rebellion 1850–1864; the first battle was in late December 1850 and the Jintian rout and Hong’s proclamation in January 1851. End 1864 (fall of Nanjing); the later resistance (to January 1866 in Guangdong, the last army destroyed in August 1871) is in the text and events.

Death toll: the lead gives 20–30 million (5–10% of the population) to 73–100 million (about 25%); the Death toll section gives 20 to 30 million as the most widely cited and ‘some analysts’ up to 100 million, mostly from plague and famine. Both stated. ‘One million executed’ in Guangdong is hedged as ‘reported’ because the article says ‘Reportedly … it is written that’.

Atrocities named as the article names them: Taiping massacres of Manchus (all Manchu men killed at Nanjing, the women burned; about 40,000 Manchu civilians; 10,000 at Cangzhou, not used), Qing massacres of civilians at Nanjing and of Hakkas in Guangdong, the Xiang Army’s scorched earth and refusal to take prisoners (not used for length), destruction of farmland and cities on both sides. The article calls the Taiping massacres of Manchus ‘genocidal’ in one sentence; I wrote ‘killed the Manchu population of every area they took’.

Hong’s death: the lead says June 1, 1864, from eating weeds, with suspicions of poison; the body says food poisoning from wild vegetables, possibly suicide, after a 20-day illness. I gave only ‘died in June 1864’.

Left out as doubtful or inconsistent: Hangzhou ‘taken on March 19, 1860’ (the same day and month as Nanjing in 1853, and Hangzhou is captured again on 31 December 1861); the Battle of Muddy Flat claim that the British and Americans ‘teamed up with the Taiping’; Hong Tianguifu ‘soon caught’ versus captured on October 25, 1864; the American weapons shipment of 895 field guns.

The Taiping capital is called Tianjing and the 1856 killings the Tianjing Incident; the article also speaks of ‘an attempted coup in September and October 1856’ (Wei’s plan to imprison Hong), summarised as ‘the killings of 1856’.

Wanted but not in the article: the land system’s details (the Heavenly Land System is not named), the Taiping examination system, numbers of Western troops; the Nian and Panthay links are only alluded to via Spence.
